q: Under the step-ladder (step) method of secondary distribution of overheads:

options.A: Service departments serve each other repeatedly until the residual balances become negligible
options.B: The costs of service departments are ignored altogether
options.C: All service departments are apportioned simultaneously by means of simultaneous equations
options.D: The service departments are arranged in a sequence and apportioned one after another, a department once closed receiving no further apportionment

e: In the step method, service departments are ranked in a sequence and their costs are apportioned downwards one by one; once a department is closed, it receives no share of the apportionments that follow.

q: A predetermined overhead absorption rate, based on budgeted overheads and the budgeted level of the absorption base, is used mainly because:

options.A: It gives the exact actual cost of each job executed
options.B: It enables jobs to be costed promptly without waiting for the actual overheads, and avoids wide fluctuations in unit cost from month to month
options.C: It eliminates the need for preparing budgets
options.D: It guarantees that the overheads will be exactly absorbed

e: A predetermined rate lets each job be costed promptly on completion using budgeted overheads and activity, instead of waiting for period-end actuals; it also avoids wide month-to-month fluctuations in unit cost.

q: Under absorption costing, the closing stock of finished goods is valued at:

options.C: Full cost of production, including a share of fixed production overheads
options.D: Selling price less selling and distribution expenses

e: Absorption costing charges both variable and fixed production overheads to products, so closing stock is carried at full cost of production, including its share of fixed production overheads.

q: The basic reason why the profit under absorption costing differs from the profit under marginal costing is that:

options.A: Fixed production overheads are carried forward in the value of closing stock under absorption costing, whereas under marginal costing they are charged in full against the profit of the period
options.B: Variable costs are measured differently under the two methods
options.C: Selling overheads are ignored under marginal costing
options.D: Depreciation is not charged under absorption costing

e: Under absorption costing, fixed production overheads are carried forward in closing stock to the next period; under marginal costing they are charged in full against the period's profit, which causes the difference.

q: A product sells for Rs 150 per unit. Its variable cost per unit is: material Rs 50, labour Rs 30 and variable overheads Rs 20. Fixed costs are Rs 2,00,000 and 8,000 units are sold. The profit under marginal costing is:
e: Contribution per unit = 150 - (50 + 30 + 20) = Rs 50. Total contribution = 50 x 8,000 = Rs 4,00,000. Profit = 4,00,000 - 2,00,000 = Rs 2,00,000.

q: A product sells for Rs 250 per unit with a variable cost of Rs 150 per unit. Fixed costs are Rs 3,60,000. The break-even sales value is:
e: P/V ratio = (250 - 150) / 250 = 40%. Break-even sales = Fixed costs / P/V ratio = 3,60,000 / 0.40 = Rs 9,00,000.

q: The margin of safety of a business can be improved by:

options.A: Increasing sales volume, reducing fixed costs or reducing the variable cost per unit
options.B: Increasing the fixed costs of the business
options.C: Reducing the selling price without any change in costs or volume
options.D: Increasing the break-even point of the business

e: Margin of safety is the excess of actual sales over break-even sales; it widens when sales increase or when the break-even point falls through lower fixed costs or lower variable cost per unit.

q: In break-even analysis, when the margin of safety (in sales value) and the P/V ratio are known, the profit is computed as:

options.A: Margin of safety multiplied by total fixed costs
options.B: Margin of safety divided by the P/V ratio
options.C: Total sales multiplied by the P/V ratio
options.D: Margin of safety multiplied by the P/V ratio

e: Profit arises only on sales above the break-even level, that is, on the margin of safety; hence Profit = Margin of safety (in sales value) x P/V ratio.

q: The P/V ratio of a firm is 50% and its fixed costs are Rs 3,60,000. The sales required to earn a profit equal to 20% of sales are:
If the selling price of a product is increased while its variable cost per unit and total fixed costs remain unchanged, the break-even point will:

options.B: Decrease, because the contribution per unit increases

e: A higher selling price increases the contribution per unit while fixed costs remain unchanged, so the fixed costs are recovered with fewer units and the break-even point decreases.

q: Raw material is the limiting factor in a factory. Product A gives a contribution of Rs 90 per unit and consumes 3 kg of material per unit; Product B gives a contribution of Rs 120 per unit and consumes 5 kg of material per unit. Production priority should be given to:

options.A: Product A, because its contribution per kg of material (Rs 30) is higher
options.B: Product B, because its contribution per unit is higher
options.C: Product B, because it consumes more material per unit

e: With a scarce resource, products are ranked by contribution per unit of the limiting factor. A gives 90 / 3 = Rs 30 per kg against B's 120 / 5 = Rs 24 per kg, so A gets priority.

q: A factory has 9,000 kg of a scarce material. Product A requires 3 kg per unit, gives a contribution of Rs 90 per unit and has a maximum demand of 2,000 units. Product B requires 5 kg per unit and gives a contribution of Rs 100 per unit. After meeting the full demand for A, the number of units of B that can be produced is:
e: A uses 2,000 x 3 = 6,000 kg for its full demand. Material left = 9,000 - 6,000 = 3,000 kg, giving B = 3,000 / 5 = 600 units.

q: A component is required in 10,000 units per year. Making it in-house involves a variable cost of Rs 24 per unit and specific fixed costs of Rs 30,000 per year, which would be wholly avoided if the component were bought. An outside supplier offers it at Rs 30 per unit. The correct decision is to:

options.A: Buy, because the purchase price is recovered from the customers in the selling price
options.B: Make, because the total relevant cost of making (Rs 2,70,000) is less than the cost of buying (Rs 3,00,000)
options.C: Buy, because the supplier's price of Rs 30 per unit is a firm quoted price
options.D: Remain indifferent, as the two alternatives cost the same

e: Relevant cost of making = (10,000 x 24) + 30,000 avoidable fixed cost = Rs 2,70,000, against buying at 10,000 x 30 = Rs 3,00,000. Making is cheaper by Rs 30,000.

q: Which of the following is a qualitative (non-financial) factor in a make-or-buy decision?

options.A: The variable cost of making the component
options.B: The purchase price quoted by the outside supplier
options.C: The degree of control the firm retains over the quality and timely supply of the component
options.D: The fixed costs that will continue even if the component is bought

e: Control over the quality and timely supply of the component is a qualitative, non-financial consideration; the other options are monetary amounts that enter the relevant-cost comparison directly.

q: A firm has spare capacity. Its variable cost is Rs 48 per unit. It receives a one-time special order for 3,000 units at Rs 55 per unit, involving no extra fixed cost. The order should be:

options.A: Accepted, because it adds Rs 21,000 to the profit of the firm
options.B: Rejected, because the price offered is below the normal selling price
options.C: Accepted only if the price is raised to cover the full cost per unit
options.D: Rejected, because special orders reduce the margin of safety

e: With spare capacity and no extra fixed cost, only variable cost is relevant: incremental gain = 3,000 x (55 - 48) = Rs 21,000, so the order adds to profit and should be accepted.

q: When a firm is already working at full capacity, a special order should be accepted only if its price covers:

options.A: The variable cost of the order alone
options.B: The variable cost plus an equal share of the fixed costs
options.C: Only the direct material cost of the order
options.D: The variable cost plus the contribution that would be lost on the regular work displaced by the order

e: At full capacity the order displaces regular work, so the contribution lost on that displaced work is an opportunity cost and must be covered by the order's price in addition to its variable cost.

q: The total fixed costs of a plant are Rs 3,00,000 per year, of which Rs 1,20,000 would continue to be incurred even during a shutdown. The contribution is Rs 45 per unit. The shutdown point is:
e: Shutdown point = Avoidable fixed costs / Contribution per unit = (3,00,000 - 1,20,000) / 45 = 1,80,000 / 45 = 4,000 units; below this output, shutting down results in a smaller loss.

q: In deciding whether to shut down a plant temporarily during a period of very low demand, the relevant comparison is between:

options.A: The total cost of the plant and its total revenue
options.B: The loss if the plant is operated and the loss if it is shut — the latter consisting of the unavoidable fixed costs plus the costs of closing down and of re-opening
options.C: The fixed costs and the variable costs of the plant
options.D: The book value of the plant and its market value

e: The decision compares the loss if the plant is operated with the loss if it is shut, the latter being the unavoidable fixed costs plus the costs of closing down and re-opening.

q: The standard price of a material is Rs 15 per kg and the actual price paid is Rs 14 per kg. The actual quantity consumed is 3,000 kg. The material price variance is:
e: Material price variance = (Standard price - Actual price) x Actual quantity = (15 - 14) x 3,000 = Rs 3,000 (Favourable), because the actual price paid is lower than standard.

q: For the actual output, the standard quantity of material is 800 kg, but the actual quantity consumed is 750 kg. The standard price is Rs 12 per kg. The material usage variance is:
e: Material usage variance = (Standard quantity - Actual quantity) x Standard price = (800 - 750) x 12 = Rs 600 (Favourable), because less material was consumed than the standard allowance.

q: The standard wage rate is Rs 45 per hour and the actual rate paid is Rs 48 per hour for 800 actual hours worked. The labour rate variance is:
e: Labour rate variance = (Standard rate - Actual rate) x Actual hours = (45 - 48) x 800 = Rs 2,400 (Adverse), because a higher wage rate than standard was paid.

q: For the actual output, the standard labour time is 900 hours, but 1,000 hours were actually taken. The standard rate is Rs 25 per hour. The labour efficiency variance is:
e: Labour efficiency variance = (Standard hours - Actual hours) x Standard rate = (900 - 1,000) x 25 = Rs 2,500 (Adverse), because more hours were taken than the standard time allowed.

q: The fixed overhead expenditure (budget) variance is the difference between:

options.A: The budgeted fixed overheads and the actual fixed overheads incurred
options.B: The fixed overheads absorbed and the budgeted fixed overheads
options.C: The budgeted output and the actual output of the period
options.D: The standard hours and the actual hours worked

e: The fixed overhead expenditure (budget) variance compares budgeted fixed overheads with the actual fixed overheads incurred; it measures spending control alone, before any volume or absorption effects.

q: In process costing, an abnormal gain arises when:

options.A: The actual output of the process is less than the input
options.B: The scrap of the process realises more than its expected value
options.C: The cost of the process exceeds the budgeted cost
options.D: The actual loss in the process is less than the normal loss expected, so that the actual output exceeds the expected output; the gain is valued at the cost per unit of good output

e: When the actual loss is less than the normal loss expected, output exceeds the expected output and the excess good units form an abnormal gain, valued at the cost per unit of good output.

q: A by-product, as distinguished from a joint product, is a product which:

options.A: Is the main product for the manufacture of which the process is run
options.B: Arises incidentally in the course of manufacturing the main product and is of relatively small sales value
options.C: Always has no sales value and must necessarily be scrapped
options.D: Is necessarily produced in a separate subsequent process

e: A by-product arises incidentally in manufacturing the main product and is of relatively small sales value, unlike a joint product, which is itself one of the major outputs of the joint process.

q: In a process, 2,500 units are introduced at a total cost of Rs 63,000. Normal loss is 20% of input and the scrap realises Rs 6 per unit. The cost per unit of good output is:
e: Good output = 2,500 less 20% normal loss = 2,000 units. Net cost = 63,000 - (500 x 6) = Rs 60,000. Cost per unit = 60,000 / 2,000 = Rs 30.00.

q: A goods transport undertaking incurs a total operating cost of Rs 7,50,000 during a period in which it performs 25,00,000 tonne-kilometres. The cost per tonne-kilometre is:
e: Cost per tonne-kilometre = Total operating cost / Total tonne-kilometres performed = 7,50,000 / 25,00,000 = Rs 0.30.

q: In transport costing, which of the following is a running (operating) charge, varying with the distance run?
e: Running charges vary with the distance run; fuel and lubricants are consumed per kilometre, whereas insurance premium, licence fee and garage rent are standing charges that accrue with time.

q: Under activity-based costing, batch-level activities are those which:

options.A: Are performed for each individual unit produced, such as machining
options.B: Support the factory as a whole, such as plant management and security
options.C: Are performed for each product line, such as product design and engineering
options.D: Are performed each time a batch is processed — such as machine set-ups, first-item inspection and materials movement — regardless of the number of units in the batch

e: Batch-level activities are performed each time a batch is processed, such as machine set-ups, first-item inspection and materials movement, and their cost does not depend on the number of units in the batch.

q: Under activity-based costing, the inspection cost pool of a plant is Rs 2,40,000 and the total number of inspections in the period is 1,200. A product requiring 300 inspections will be assigned inspection cost of:
e: Cost driver rate = 2,40,000 / 1,200 inspections = Rs 200 per inspection. Inspection cost assigned to the product = 300 x 200 = Rs 60,000.

q: A project requires an initial outlay of Rs 4,00,000 and is expected to yield a net cash inflow of Rs 1,20,000 at the end of each of the next 5 years. The cumulative present value (annuity) factor for 5 years at 10% is 3.791. The Net Present Value of the project is:
e: Present value of inflows = 1,20,000 x 3.791 = Rs 4,54,920. NPV = 4,54,920 - 4,00,000 = (+) Rs 54,920, so the project is acceptable.

q: The present value of the future cash inflows of a project is Rs 3,60,000 and its initial investment is Rs 3,00,000. The Profitability Index of the project is:
e: Profitability Index = Present value of cash inflows / Initial investment = 3,60,000 / 3,00,000 = 1.20; an index above 1 corresponds to a positive NPV.

q: A project involves an initial outlay of Rs 2,75,000. The discounted (present) values of its cash inflows are Rs 1,00,000 at the end of Year 1, Rs 1,00,000 at the end of Year 2 and Rs 1,00,000 at the end of Year 3. The discounted payback period of the project is:
e: Discounted inflows cumulate to Rs 2,00,000 by the end of Year 2; Rs 75,000 more is needed out of Year 3's Rs 1,00,000, i.e., 9 months. Discounted payback = 2 years 9 months.

q: A firm has already spent Rs 50,000 on a feasibility study for a proposed project. In appraising the project, this expenditure should be:

options.A: Treated as a sunk cost and excluded from the project's incremental cash flows
options.B: Added to the initial capital cost of the project
options.C: Charged as an annual operating cost over the life of the project
options.D: Recovered from the agency that conducted the study

e: The feasibility study expenditure is already incurred and irrecoverable whether or not the project proceeds; as a sunk cost it is excluded from the project's incremental cash flows.

q: A proposed project requires land already owned by the enterprise, which could alternatively be sold for Rs 2,00,000. In appraising the project, this amount of Rs 2,00,000 should be:

options.A: Ignored, since no cash payment is involved
options.B: Treated as a cost (cash outflow) of the project, being its opportunity cost
options.C: Treated as a benefit of the project
options.D: Recorded only in the notes to the accounts

e: Using the owned land for the project sacrifices its sale value of Rs 2,00,000; this forgone benefit is the opportunity cost of the land and is treated as a cash outflow of the project.

q: A project involves annual depreciation of Rs 40,000 on its plant. The tax rate is 30%. The annual tax shield (tax saving) provided by this depreciation is:
e: Depreciation is a tax-deductible expense, so it saves tax of 40,000 x 30% = Rs 12,000 every year; this depreciation tax shield is a benefit attributable to the project.

q:
Consider the following statements:
1. If a project's internal rate of return is exactly equal to the enterprise's cost of capital, its net present value is zero.
2. In that situation, the Profitability Index of the project is exactly 1.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
e: Both statements are correct: discounting at the IRR makes NPV zero by definition, and the Profitability Index equals exactly 1 when the present value of inflows just equals the investment, i.e., NPV is zero.

q: The terminal (final-year) cash flow of a project normally includes:

options.A: The salvage value of the plant and the recovery of the working capital invested in the project
options.B: The depreciation charged in the final year of the project
options.C: The initial cost of the project
options.D: The book value of assets scrapped without any sale

e: In the final year the plant is sold, realising its salvage value, and the working capital invested in the project is recovered; both form part of the terminal cash flow.

q: Where a number of projects are independent of each other and there is no shortage of funds, the correct capital budgeting decision is to accept:

options.A: Only the project with the highest internal rate of return
options.B: Only the project with the shortest payback period
options.C: Only one project, whichever is the cheapest
options.D: All projects with a positive net present value

e: Where projects are independent and funds are unlimited, every positive-NPV project adds to the enterprise's wealth, so all such projects should be accepted, not only the single best one.

q: An investment of Rs 8,00,000, with no salvage value, is expected to yield an average annual profit after depreciation and tax of Rs 80,000. The Average Rate of Return on the initial investment is:
e: ARR on initial investment = Average annual profit after depreciation and tax / Initial investment x 100 = 80,000 / 8,00,000 x 100 = 10%.

q: A project costing Rs 7,20,000 yields net cash inflows of Rs 2,40,000 in Year 1, Rs 2,40,000 in Year 2 and Rs 3,60,000 in Year 3. Its payback period is:
e: Cumulative inflows are Rs 2,40,000 in Year 1 and Rs 4,80,000 by Year 2; Rs 2,40,000 more is needed out of Year 3's Rs 3,60,000, i.e., 8 months. Payback = 2 years 8 months.

q: The earnings per share of a company are Rs 8 and the market price of its share is Rs 80. Under the earnings-price (E/P) approach, the cost of equity capital is:
e: Under the E/P approach, cost of equity = Earnings per share / Market price per share = 8 / 80 = 10%; the market price is viewed as earnings capitalised at this rate.

q: A company issues 10% debentures at par. If the tax rate is 40%, the after-tax cost of debt is:
e: Interest on debentures is tax-deductible, so the after-tax cost of debt = 10% x (1 - 0.40) = 6%.

q: A company's capital structure consists of debt of Rs 3,00,000 with an after-tax cost of 6% and equity of Rs 7,00,000 with a cost of 13%. Its weighted average cost of capital is:
The cost of retained earnings, as compared with the cost of new equity share capital, is generally:

options.A: Higher, because retained earnings belong to the shareholders
options.B: Zero, because no payment is made for their use
options.C: Slightly lower, because no issue (flotation) costs are incurred in using them
options.D: Equal to the after-tax cost of debt

e: Retained earnings involve no issue or flotation costs such as brokerage and underwriting, which a fresh issue of shares must bear; hence they cost slightly less than new equity capital.

q: If an enterprise uses the same overall weighted average cost of capital as the discount rate for appraising all projects, irrespective of the risk of each project, the likely consequence is that it may:

options.A: Accept some high-risk projects that destroy value and reject some safe, worthwhile projects
options.B: Always maximise the value of the enterprise
options.C: Avoid the need for project appraisal altogether

e: Using one average WACC over-discounts safe projects and under-discounts risky ones; the enterprise may therefore accept high-risk projects that destroy value while rejecting safe projects that would create it.

q: Sales of an enterprise are Rs 15,00,000, variable costs are Rs 9,00,000 and fixed costs are Rs 4,00,000. The degree of operating leverage is:
An enterprise has earnings before interest and tax of Rs 6,00,000 and pays interest of Rs 2,00,000. Its degree of financial leverage is:
e: Degree of financial leverage = EBIT / (EBIT - Interest) = 6,00,000 / (6,00,000 - 2,00,000) = 6,00,000 / 4,00,000 = 1.5.

q: The degree of combined leverage is equal to:

options.A: Degree of operating leverage + degree of financial leverage
options.B: Degree of operating leverage - degree of financial leverage
options.C: Degree of financial leverage divided by degree of operating leverage
options.D: Degree of operating leverage x degree of financial leverage

e: Combined leverage captures the joint effect of operating and financial leverage on earnings per share, and the two degrees multiply: DCL = DOL x DFL.

q: At the break-even point, the degree of operating leverage is:

options.A: Infinite (undefined), because operating profit at that point is zero
options.D: Equal to the degree of financial leverage

e: Degree of operating leverage = Contribution / Operating profit. At the break-even point operating profit is zero, so the leverage is infinite (undefined).

q: An enterprise has sales of Rs 20,00,000, variable costs of Rs 12,00,000, fixed costs of Rs 3,00,000 and interest of Rs 3,00,000. Its degree of combined leverage is:
e: Contribution = 20,00,000 - 12,00,000 = Rs 8,00,000; EBT = 8,00,000 - 3,00,000 fixed costs - 3,00,000 interest = Rs 2,00,000. Degree of combined leverage = 8,00,000 / 2,00,000 = 4.0.

q: The capital gearing ratio is computed as:

options.A: Current assets divided by current liabilities
options.B: Fixed assets divided by net worth
options.C: (Preference share capital + debentures and long-term loans) divided by equity shareholders' funds
options.D: Total debt divided by total assets

e: Capital gearing compares the fixed-cost capital - preference share capital plus debentures and long-term loans - with equity shareholders' funds, showing how far the structure rests on fixed-charge funds.

q: Current assets of an enterprise are Rs 7,50,000 and its current liabilities are Rs 3,00,000. Its current ratio is:
e: Current ratio = Current assets / Current liabilities = 7,50,000 / 3,00,000 = 2.5 : 1.

q: Long-term debt of an enterprise is Rs 9,00,000 and its shareholders' funds are Rs 6,00,000. The debt-equity ratio is:
e: Debt-equity ratio = Long-term debt / Shareholders' funds = 9,00,000 / 6,00,000 = 1.5 : 1.

q: Credit sales of an enterprise are Rs 9,60,000 and its average debtors are Rs 1,20,000. The debtors turnover ratio is:
e: Debtors turnover ratio = Credit sales / Average debtors = 9,60,000 / 1,20,000 = 8 times.

q: The cost of goods sold of an enterprise is Rs 9,00,000 and its average inventory is Rs 1,50,000. The inventory turnover ratio is:
e: Inventory turnover ratio = Cost of goods sold / Average inventory = 9,00,000 / 1,50,000 = 6 times.

q: Sales of an enterprise are Rs 16,00,000 and the cost of goods sold is Rs 10,40,000. Its gross profit ratio is:
The net profit of an enterprise is Rs 90,000 on sales of Rs 12,00,000. Its net profit ratio is:
e: Net profit ratio = Net profit / Sales x 100 = 90,000 / 12,00,000 x 100 = 7.5%.

q: The profit before interest and tax of an enterprise is Rs 3,00,000 and its capital employed is Rs 12,00,000. The Return on Capital Employed is:
e: Return on Capital Employed = Profit before interest and tax / Capital employed x 100 = 3,00,000 / 12,00,000 x 100 = 25%.

q: The profit before interest and tax of an enterprise is Rs 7,50,000 and the interest payable is Rs 2,50,000. The interest coverage ratio is:
e: Interest coverage ratio = Profit before interest and tax / Interest payable = 7,50,000 / 2,50,000 = 3 times.

q: Current assets of an enterprise are Rs 10,00,000, including stock of Rs 4,00,000 and prepaid expenses of Rs 1,00,000. Current liabilities are Rs 4,00,000. The quick (acid-test) ratio is:
e: Quick assets = 10,00,000 - 4,00,000 stock - 1,00,000 prepaid expenses = Rs 5,00,000. Quick ratio = 5,00,000 / 4,00,000 = 1.25 : 1.

q: The net profit after tax of a company is Rs 7,20,000 and the preference dividend payable is Rs 1,20,000. If the company has 1,50,000 equity shares, its Earnings Per Share (EPS) is:
e: EPS = (Net profit after tax - Preference dividend) / Number of equity shares = (7,20,000 - 1,20,000) / 1,50,000 = Rs 4.00.

q: A company's Dividend Per Share is Rs 5 and the market price of its share is Rs 80. Its dividend yield ratio is:
e: Dividend yield ratio = Dividend per share / Market price per share x 100 = 5 / 80 x 100 = 6.25%.

q: 'Window dressing' of a balance sheet means:

options.A: Manipulating the position at the year-end, e.g., by paying off creditors just before the balance-sheet date, so as to present a better picture than the reality
options.B: Getting the balance sheet audited by external auditors
options.D: Comparing the ratios of the enterprise with industry averages

e: Window dressing is the deliberate manipulation of the year-end position, for example paying off creditors just before the balance-sheet date, so that ratios present a better picture than the reality.

q: Which of the following transactions involves a flow of funds?

options.B: Issue of bonus shares out of the general reserve
options.C: Acquisition of machinery by issuing debentures

e: Redeeming debentures for cash reduces both long-term debt and a current asset, changing working capital, so it is a flow of funds; the other transactions move only non-current items among themselves.

q: In a cash flow statement, the cash inflow on the sale of machinery is taken as:

options.A: The book value of the machinery
options.C: Only the profit earned on the sale
options.D: The original cost of the machinery

e: A cash flow statement reports actual cash movements, so the sale of machinery is shown at the actual sale proceeds received, not at its book value, original cost or the profit element alone.

q: An enterprise's operating profit before working capital changes is Rs 2,00,000. During the year, its debtors increased by Rs 30,000 and its creditors increased by Rs 20,000. The cash from operations is:
e: Cash from operations = 2,00,000 - 30,000 for the increase in debtors, which ties up cash, + 20,000 for the increase in creditors, which defers payment = Rs 1,90,000.

q: In the schedule of changes in working capital, a decrease in debtors (a current asset) during the year results in:

options.D: An increase in funds from operations

e: In the schedule of changes in working capital, working capital moves in the same direction as current assets; a decrease in debtors reduces current assets and therefore decreases working capital.

q: The net profit of an enterprise is Rs 2,50,000, after charging depreciation of Rs 45,000 and a loss of Rs 5,000 on the sale of furniture, and after crediting a profit of Rs 20,000 on the sale of investments. The funds from operations are:
e: Funds from operations = 2,50,000 + 45,000 depreciation + 5,000 loss on sale of furniture - 20,000 profit on sale of investments = Rs 2,80,000, after adjusting non-cash and non-operating items.

q: Under Accounting Standard 3 (AS-3), cash flows from taxes on income are ordinarily classified as:

options.B: Operating activities, unless they can be specifically identified with investing or financing activities
options.D: Not shown in the cash flow statement at all

e: Under AS-3, cash flows from taxes on income are classified as operating activities unless they can be specifically identified with financing or investing activities.

q: 'Cash equivalents' in a cash flow statement are:

options.A: All investments held by the enterprise
options.C: Only the cash balance in hand
options.D: Short-term, highly liquid investments that are readily convertible into known amounts of cash and subject to an insignificant risk of change in value

e: Cash equivalents are short-term, highly liquid investments that are readily convertible into known amounts of cash and are subject to an insignificant risk of changes in value.

q: In computing the anticipated rate of return on a proposed railway work, the credit taken on the earnings side includes:

options.A: Additional earnings from the work plus savings in working expenses expected from it, after deducting the additional working expenses
options.B: Only the additional earnings from new traffic
options.C: Only the savings in working expenses
options.D: The gross earnings of the entire railway

e: The earnings credited in the rate-of-return computation are net in nature: additional earnings from the work plus savings in working expenses, after deducting the additional working expenses the work itself causes.

q: A proposed new railway line fails the prescribed financial test of remunerativeness. In such a case, the line:

options.A: Can never be sanctioned in any circumstances
options.B: Is sanctioned automatically if any State Government supports it
options.C: May still be sanctioned on strategic or developmental considerations, its justification then resting on economic rather than purely financial returns
options.D: Must be executed only through a public-private partnership concession

e: A line failing the financial test of remunerativeness may still be sanctioned on strategic or developmental considerations, in which case its justification rests on economic rather than purely financial returns.

q: The rate of dividend payable by Indian Railways to General Revenues on its capital-at-charge is determined on the recommendations of the:

options.D: Comptroller and Auditor General of India

e: The dividend rate payable by Indian Railways to General Revenues on capital-at-charge is fixed on the recommendations of the Railway Convention Committee, which periodically reviews the railway finances.

q: Financial justification (rate-of-return appraisal) is NOT required for:

options.D: Ordinary revenue (working) expenditure, which does not create a capital asset

e: Financial justification by rate-of-return appraisal applies to capital works that create assets; ordinary revenue (working) expenditure creates no capital asset and so does not require such justification.

q: A budget provides for fixed costs of Rs 2,40,000 and variable costs of Rs 18 per unit at a budgeted output of 20,000 units. The flexed budget allowance for an actual output of 16,000 units is:
e: In the flexed budget, fixed costs stay at Rs 2,40,000 and only the variable element moves with output: allowance = 2,40,000 + (18 x 16,000) = 2,40,000 + 2,88,000 = Rs 5,28,000.

q: Budgeted sales of a product are 40,000 units. The opening stock of finished goods is 6,000 units and the desired closing stock is 4,000 units. The production budget should provide for production of:
e: Production budget = Budgeted sales + Desired closing stock - Opening stock = 40,000 + 4,000 - 6,000 = 38,000 units.

q: Production of 30,000 units is budgeted, each unit requiring 3 kg of material. The opening stock of material is 8,000 kg and the closing stock is to be 10,000 kg. The quantity of material to be purchased is:
e: Material required for production = 30,000 x 3 = 90,000 kg. Purchases = 90,000 + 10,000 desired closing stock - 8,000 opening stock = 92,000 kg.

q: A cash budget for a month shows an opening cash balance of Rs 25,000, estimated receipts of Rs 3,40,000 and estimated payments of Rs 3,15,000. The closing cash balance will be:
e: Closing cash balance = Opening balance + Estimated receipts - Estimated payments = 25,000 + 3,40,000 - 3,15,000 = Rs 50,000.

q: A semi-variable cost amounts to Rs 60,000 at an output of 5,000 units and Rs 75,000 at an output of 8,000 units. The variable element per unit is:
e: Variable element per unit = Change in cost / Change in output = (75,000 - 60,000) / (8,000 - 5,000) = 15,000 / 3,000 = Rs 5 per unit.

q: Long-range (strategic) planning differs from annual budgeting mainly in that long-range planning:

options.A: Is prepared by the accounts department only
options.B: Covers a longer horizon of several years and is concerned with broad strategies and objectives, whereas the budget is a detailed short-term plan, usually for one year
options.C: Is not concerned with financial figures at all

e: Long-range planning covers several years and deals with broad strategies and objectives, whereas annual budgeting is a detailed plan, usually for one year, framed within that longer-term framework.

q: Under incremental budgeting:

options.A: Every item of expenditure is justified afresh from a zero base
options.C: Budgets are prepared only when the level of activity changes
options.D: The previous year's budget or actuals are taken as the base and adjusted for known changes, so that existing inefficiencies may be carried forward

e: Under incremental budgeting, the previous year's budget or actuals form the base and are adjusted only for known changes; because the base is never re-examined, existing inefficiencies may be carried forward.

q: The Outcome Budget differs from the traditional Performance Budget mainly in that the Outcome Budget measures:

options.A: The inputs consumed by a programme
options.B: The physical outputs produced by a programme
options.C: The final results and impact of the expenditure on the intended beneficiaries, rather than merely the outputs produced
options.D: Only the savings achieved against the grants

e: The Outcome Budget goes beyond the physical outputs measured by a Performance Budget and measures the final results and impact of the expenditure on the intended beneficiaries.

q: 'Participative' (bottom-up) budgeting means that:

options.A: Budgets are prepared with the active involvement of the managers who will be responsible for achieving them, which generally improves motivation and commitment to the targets
options.B: Budgets are imposed by the top management without any consultation
options.C: Only the finance department participates in budget preparation
options.D: Workers participate in the statutory audit of the enterprise

e: Participative budgeting involves the managers responsible for achieving the targets in preparing them; this involvement generally improves the realism of the budget and their motivation and commitment to it.

q: Under the replacement cost approach to human resource accounting, the value of the human resources of an organisation is measured by:

options.A: The present value of the future earnings of the employees up to retirement
options.B: The cost that would have to be incurred to replace the existing employees with persons of equivalent experience and efficiency
options.C: The total salaries paid to the employees since their appointment
options.D: The market capitalisation of the organisation

e: Under the replacement cost approach, human resources are valued at the cost that would have to be incurred to replace the present employees with persons of equivalent experience and efficiency.

q: Current assets of an enterprise are Rs 9,00,000 and its current liabilities are Rs 4,50,000. Its net working capital is:
e: Net working capital = Current assets - Current liabilities = 9,00,000 - 4,50,000 = Rs 4,50,000.

q: In a manufacturing concern, raw materials are held for 40 days, the production process takes 20 days, finished goods are held for 25 days and customers take 50 days to pay. Suppliers allow 35 days' credit. The length of the operating cycle is:
e: Operating cycle = 40 (raw materials) + 20 (production) + 25 (finished goods) + 50 (receivables) - 35 (suppliers' credit) = 100 days.

q: The annual operating expenses of an enterprise are Rs 36,00,000 (reckoning a year of 360 days). Its operating cycle is 90 days. On the operating-cycle method, the working capital required is:
e: Working capital required = Annual operating expenses x Operating cycle / 360 = 36,00,000 x 90 / 360 = Rs 9,00,000.

q: Under a conservative working capital financing policy:

options.A: Even a part of the permanent working capital is financed from short-term funds
options.B: Long-term funds finance the whole of the permanent working capital and also a part of the temporary working capital, so that risk and liquidity pressure are low, though the cost is higher
options.C: No working capital is maintained at all
options.D: Current assets are kept at the bare minimum level

e: Under a conservative policy, long-term funds finance the whole permanent working capital and also part of the temporary working capital; liquidity pressure is low but the cost of funds is higher.

q: Excessive working capital (more than adequate for the operations) in an enterprise generally leads to:

options.A: Frequent stock-outs and loss of sales
options.B: Inability to pay the creditors on time
options.C: Higher earnings on planned investments of surplus funds
options.D: Idle funds earning nothing, a liberal credit policy and accumulation of slow-moving stock, which reduce the overall profitability

e: Excessive working capital leaves funds idle and earning nothing, encourages a liberal credit policy and lets slow-moving stock accumulate, all of which reduce the overall profitability of the enterprise.

q: An enterprise has a negative cash conversion cycle. This means that:

options.A: It makes losses on all its cash sales
options.B: Its operating cycle cannot be computed
options.C: It collects cash from its customers before it has to pay its suppliers, so that the operations are partly financed by trade credit
options.D: It holds no inventory at all

e: A negative cash conversion cycle means the firm collects from its customers before it must pay its suppliers, so day-to-day operations are partly financed by trade credit.

q: The 'working capital gap' is:

options.A: The difference between total current assets and current liabilities other than bank borrowings, representing the portion of current assets that has to be financed from long-term sources and bank finance
options.B: The excess of fixed assets over long-term funds
options.C: The difference between gross working capital and net working capital
options.D: The amount of cash in hand at the end of the year

e: The working capital gap is total current assets minus current liabilities other than bank borrowings; it represents the portion of current assets to be financed from long-term sources and bank finance.

q: The maximum consumption of a material is 300 units per week and the maximum re-order period is 4 weeks. The re-order level for the material is:
e: Re-order level = Maximum consumption x Maximum re-order period = 300 x 4 = 1,200 units, fixed high enough to cover the longest expected lead time at the fastest usage.

q: The re-order level of a material is 2,000 units. Normal (average) consumption is 150 units per week and the normal re-order period is 6 weeks. The minimum stock level is:
e: Minimum stock level = Re-order level - (Normal consumption x Normal re-order period) = 2,000 - (150 x 6) = 2,000 - 900 = 1,100 units.

q: The re-order level of a material is 1,800 units and the re-order quantity is 1,500 units. Minimum consumption is 100 units per week and the minimum re-order period is 5 weeks. The maximum stock level is:
e: Maximum stock level = Re-order level + Re-order quantity - (Minimum consumption x Minimum re-order period) = 1,800 + 1,500 - (100 x 5) = 2,800 units.

q: The minimum stock level of a material is 900 units and the re-order quantity is 1,400 units. The average stock level is:
e: Average stock level = Minimum stock level + Half the re-order quantity = 900 + (1,400 / 2) = 1,600 units.

q: The 'danger level' of a stock item is fixed as:

options.A: Maximum consumption multiplied by the maximum re-order period
options.B: Average (normal) consumption multiplied by the maximum re-order period allowed for emergency purchases; on reaching it, special efforts are made to obtain supplies
options.C: Minimum consumption multiplied by the minimum re-order period
options.D: The level at which the stores are closed for annual stock verification

e: The danger level is fixed as average (normal) consumption multiplied by the maximum re-order period allowed for emergency purchases; on reaching it, special efforts are made to obtain supplies urgently.

q: The annual consumption of a material is 3,600 units. The cost of placing an order is Rs 50 and the carrying cost is Rs 4 per unit per year. Using EOQ = sqrt(2AO/C), the Economic Order Quantity is:
e: EOQ = sqrt(2 x 3,600 x 50 / 4) = sqrt(90,000) = 300 units, the order quantity at which total ordering and carrying costs are minimised.

q: The annual credit sales of an enterprise are Rs 9,00,000 and its average debtors are Rs 1,00,000. Taking a year of 360 days, the average collection period is:
e: Average collection period = Average debtors / Annual credit sales x 360 = 1,00,000 / 9,00,000 x 360 = 40 days.

q: Credit sales of an enterprise are Rs 10,80,000 and its average debtors are Rs 1,35,000. The debtors turnover ratio is:
e: Debtors turnover ratio = Credit sales / Average debtors = 10,80,000 / 1,35,000 = 8 times.
